body:
Ep. 01 · Snap a glow stick and it lights up with no battery, no bulb and no wire. Inside the tube floats a thin glass vial of hydrogen peroxide. Bend it, the glass cracks, and the peroxide meets diphenyl oxalate. They build a very unstable molecule that falls apart into carbon dioxide and hands its energy to a dye, which gives it off as light. That's cold light: almost no heat. Warm it up and it glows brighter but quits sooner; cool it down and it lasts longer. 🎃

Sources: Wikipedia "Glow stick" and "Chemiluminescence"; Compound Interest "The Chemistry of Glow Sticks"; Temple University Chemistry Demos "Chemiluminescence" (2024).

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 02 · Two dots and a line, and your brain yells: face! That's pareidolia. Your brain runs an always-on face detector: your eyes can start moving toward a face in about a tenth of a second, and a 2020 brain-scan study found face-like objects handled by the brain's face areas, before being sorted back into plain objects within about a quarter of a second. Monkeys do it too, and in one study babies still in the womb turned toward a face-shaped pattern of three dots. Scientists describe the detector as tuned to never miss, even at the cost of false alarms. So that ghost in the curtains? Your face detector, doing its job. Where's the strangest face you've ever spotted?

Sources: Wardle et al., Nature Communications (2020); Crouzet, Kirchner & Thorpe, Journal of Vision (2010); Taubert et al., Current Biology (2017); Reid et al., Current Biology (2017); University of Sydney (Alais et al., 2021).

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 03 · Turn off the lights and at first you see nothing. Wait twenty minutes and the room slowly appears. 🌙 Your rods rebuild a light-catching pigment called rhodopsin, and you can end up as much as a million times more sensitive. One bright flash undoes it, which is why pilots and ship crews use red light. Could you sit in the dark for twenty minutes?

Sources: Webvision (Univ. of Utah, NCBI Bookshelf) "Light and Dark Adaptation"; Univ. of Minnesota "Sensation and Perception"; Wikipedia "Adaptation (eye)" and "Rod cell".

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 04 · Some mushrooms glow in the dark, with no battery and no fire. People call it foxfire: Aristotle wrote about its cold light, and it even lit the compass of the Turtle submarine in the 1770s. Inside the fungus, a fuel called luciferin reacts with oxygen, helped by an enzyme, and the energy comes out as green light. But why spend energy on light? A 2015 study in Brazil set out fake glowing mushrooms, and they drew far more insects than dark ones. Those insects may carry the spores to new wood. 🍄✨

Sources: Oliveira et al., Current Biology (2015); Kaskova et al., Science Advances (2017); Dartmouth Geisel School of Medicine; Wikipedia ("Foxfire", "Turtle (submersible)").

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 05 · Rest your fingers on a Ouija pointer and it starts to move, but nobody means to push it. In 1853 Michael Faraday tested the same mystery with séance tables: he slipped a simple pointer between the sitters' hands and the table, and it showed their own hands were pushing, ever so slightly. Once they could watch it, the table stopped turning. It's the ideomotor effect: your brain expects a movement and your muscles make it, too small to notice. No ghosts needed. 👻

Sources: Faraday, letter to The Times (June 1853); Wikipedia "Ouija" and "Ideomotor phenomenon"; The Skeptic's Dictionary "ideomotor effect"; Gauchou, Rensink & Fels, Consciousness and Cognition (2012).

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 06 · A real Halloween story: in tropical rainforests, the fungus Ophiocordyceps takes over carpenter ants. An infected ant leaves its nest high in the trees, wanders in a "drunken walk", then around noon bites the vein under a leaf about 25 cm above the ground, in humid air the fungus likes. Its jaw muscles waste away, so it stays put. Surprise: in 2017 scientists found the fungus wrapped around the ant's muscles, not in its brain. Days later a stalk grows from the back of its head and releases spores to infect more ants. Fossil leaves show the same bite marks 48 million years ago. And no, it can't infect you. Which nature fact creeps you out the most?

Sources: Hughes et al., BMC Ecology (2011); Fredericksen et al., PNAS (2017); Hughes, Wappler & Labandeira, Biology Letters (2010); NPR (2023).

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 07 · In flash photos, a cat's eyes glow, but yours turn red. Why? Behind a cat's retina is a mirror-like layer called the tapetum lucidum. Light that slips past the light-sensing cells bounces back for a second chance, which helps cats make the most of dim light (with a little blur as the price). A phone flash sits right beside the lens, so that bounced light comes straight back into the camera. People have no mirror, so the flash lights up the blood-rich layer at the back of the eye instead: red-eye. 🐈‍⬛👀

Sources: Wikipedia ("Tapetum lucidum"); Colorado State University (Dr. Cynthia Powell, veterinary ophthalmologist); Mental Floss ("Why do we get red eye in photos?").

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 08 · An owl can swoop right past you and you won't hear it. 🦉 Its wings have three tricks: a comb-like front edge, a soft fringed back edge that breaks up the turbulence, and a velvety surface that soaks up sound. Together they let the owl hear its prey without the prey hearing it coming. What would you make quieter with owl feathers?

Sources: Wikipedia "Owl"; University of Cambridge, "The owl and the wind turbine".

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 09 · One thread of spider silk can stop a flying insect, but it isn't stronger than steel. Thread for thread, good silk is about as strong as a mid-range steel; it's about six times lighter, so for its weight, silk wins. It starts as a liquid protein in the spider's glands and hardens into a fibre as it's pulled out through the spinnerets, and an orb weaver can make up to seven kinds. The real trick is the catch: the stiff spokes absorb most of the impact, much of the energy turns into heat so the bug doesn't bounce out, and the stretchy sticky spiral holds it. Walk into a web this Halloween and you'll know why it clings. Did you think silk was stronger than steel?

Sources: University of Cambridge / The Conversation, "Spider silk is a wonder of nature, but it's not stronger than steel"; Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Is spider silk stronger than steel?"; Sensenig et al., J. R. Soc. Interface (2012); Babb et al., Nature Genetics (2017).

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 10 · The October moon can rise huge and orange over the hills, but it isn't really bigger and it isn't really orange. Near the horizon, moonlight crosses much more air, which scatters the blue away (the same reason sunsets look red). And the size? Your fingernail at arm's length covers it low or high, and photos show the same width: the giant moon is an illusion in your brain. Even astronauts in orbit see it, and scientists still can't fully explain why. 🌕🍂

Sources: NASA Science ("The Moon Illusion"); NASA Astronomy Picture of the Day; StarDate (McDonald Observatory); Old Farmer's Almanac.

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 11 · Carve a pumpkin and in a few days its face starts to sag. An uncut pumpkin has a hard, waxy rind that keeps water in and germs out, and a pumpkin is about 90% water. Carving cuts right through that seal: water escapes, the flesh dries and softens, and airborne mould spores like Penicillium and Aspergillus move in with bacteria. A real candle's heat makes it worse. To slow it down, scoop out all the insides, keep it cool and out of the sun, put petroleum jelly on the cuts and use an LED light. 🎃

Sources: Utah State University Extension (2020); K-State Research and Extension (2024); Mississippi State University Extension; University of Illinois Extension.

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 12 · Your skeleton isn't spooky, it's alive and busy right now. You were born with around 300 bones that fuse into 206. They hold you up, guard your brain, heart and lungs, and let your muscles move you. Inside some bones, soft marrow is a factory for red cells, white cells and platelets. Your bones are a calcium bank, and their cells keep tearing down old bone and building new: about 10% of an adult skeleton every year. 💀🎃

Sources: Cleveland Clinic "Skeletal System"; MedlinePlus "Bone Marrow Diseases"; Healthline "How Many Bones Does a Baby Have?"; Wikipedia "Bone" and "Bone remodeling".

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 13 · Your key is a tiny code. Here is how a pin tumbler lock actually reads it 🔑 Five little pins, one shear line, and a key that lines them all up.

Sources: Britannica "Lock" and "Linus Yale, Jr."; HowStuffWorks "How Locks Work"; Wikipedia "Pin tumbler lock".

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 14 · Strike a match and fire appears, but much of the chemistry isn't on the match, it's on the box 🔥 The head holds the fuel (sulfur, antimony sulfide) and the oxygen supply (potassium chlorate). The striking strip holds red phosphorus: friction heats a trace of it, it ignites, and that sets off the head. Which everyday thing should we explain next? 👇

Sources: University of Washington Chemistry demo, Royal Society of Chemistry, Britannica, Compound Interest, AIChE CCPS.

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 15 · A steel ship weighs thousands of tons, so why doesn't it sink? Because it pushes aside its own weight in water. Clay lump vs clay boat, Archimedes' principle, average density, and the Plimsoll line, in under 90 seconds.

Sources: NASA Glenn Research Center (Buoyancy); Britannica (Archimedes' principle, Plimsoll line); OpenStax University Physics; USGS Water Science School; IMO International Convention on Load Lines; Gard.

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 16 · The Moon can hide the Sun in the middle of the day 🌑 In a solar eclipse the Moon slides between us and the Sun; its shadow has a dark inner umbra (totality) and a fainter outer penumbra. In a lunar eclipse Earth's shadow falls on the Moon, which glows dim red. Why not every month? The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5°. Safety: solar eclipses need real eclipse glasses, not sunglasses.

Sources: NASA Science, Scientific American, Earth View Inc. eclipse viewing guide.

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 17 · Why is the sky blue, a sunset red and a cloud white? It is all light scattering: tiny air molecules scatter short blue waves far more than long red ones, sunset light crosses more air so the blue is scattered out, and big cloud droplets scatter every color about equally. Here is how it really works.

Sources: Met Office, UCAR SciEd, Royal Museums Greenwich.

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 18 · Cut a magnet in half and you never get a "north piece". You get two magnets, every time. Inside iron, the electrons act like teeny magnets, and they line up in zones called domains. A nearby magnet swings those domains into line, which is why a nail sticks. Heat iron past about 770 °C and the order falls apart. Fridge magnets hide stripes of alternating poles, so they only grip on one side. So could anything ever have just one pole?

Sources: National MagLab "Magnetic Domains"; HyperPhysics (Georgia State) "Ferromagnetism"; Univ. of Illinois Physics Van; K&J Magnetics "Halbach Arrays"; CERN MoEDAL.

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 19 · A barcode doesn't hold the price or the name. All it holds is a number, and the store's computer looks up the rest. A scanner reads black bars (they soak up light) and white gaps (they bounce it back) as a signal, decodes seven-slice digits, and checks the last digit with a bit of math. The first item ever scanned was a pack of Juicy Fruit gum, in Troy, Ohio, on June 26, 1974.

Sources: GS1 (what a barcode encodes); Wikipedia "Universal Product Code" (structure, check digit, first scan, citing the Smithsonian and Wired); Scanbot and Triton (how laser scanners read bars).

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 20 · When you hit search, Google doesn't go out and search the web. It already did that. Crawlers follow links all day, and everything they find goes into an index of hundreds of billions of pages. Google compares it to the index at the back of a book. Your words pull up lists of pages, and the pages that match get ranked by meaning, relevance, quality, usability and context, all in a fraction of a second. What's the strangest thing you've ever searched?

Sources: Google "How Search works" (organizing information; ranking results); Google blog "Understanding searches better than ever before" (2019); Manning et al., Introduction to Information Retrieval.

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 21 · Your phone doesn't look at your face. It looks at its shape. Face ID projects thousands of invisible infrared dots, reads where they land to build a depth map, and turns that into numbers that stay on your device. A printed photo has no depth, so it can't fool it.

Sources: Apple Support (About Face ID advanced technology); Apple Platform Security guide (Face ID and Touch ID security).

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 22 · Your air fryer has never fried anything. 🍟 It's a tiny countertop convection oven: a heater, a fan, and air whipping around at up to 200 °C. Fast air strips away the thin "blanket" of still air around your food, the outside dries, and the Maillard reaction turns it golden. So: fryer, or very small oven?

Sources: Wikipedia "Air fryer", "Convection oven" (boundary layer), "Maillard reaction"; Philips Airfryer launch 2010, inventor Fred van der Weij (via Wikipedia).

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 23 · To reach orbit, a rocket doesn't just go up. It goes sideways. The space station moves at about 17,500 miles per hour, fast enough that as it falls toward Earth, the ground curves away beneath it. Orbit isn't escaping gravity: at the station's height, gravity is still about 90 percent as strong. It's falling and missing the ground, which is why astronauts float.

Sources: NASA (What Is Microgravity?; Space Station Facts and Figures; Basics of Space Flight, Gravity & Mechanics; Technical Memorandum TM X-52396); NOAA SciJinks.

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 24 · Out of millions of videos, only a few dozen ever reach your screen. YouTube's engineers described it as a funnel: pull out a few hundred that viewers like you enjoyed, then score each one. Back in 2011 YouTube learned that a click doesn't mean you watched, so its 2016 system predicted watch time instead, and today surveys, shares, likes and dislikes count too. Instagram says its key Reels guesses are whether you'll watch to the end, like it or reshare it. So what does your feed think you are?

Sources: Covington, Adams & Sargin, "Deep Neural Networks for YouTube Recommendations" (2016); YouTube Official Blog, "On YouTube's recommendation system" (2021); Instagram, "Instagram Ranking Explained" (2023).

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 25 · A contactless card has no battery. So how does it pay when you tap? The terminal's coil makes a magnetic field that flips about 13.5 million times a second, and it powers the card's chip through a tiny wireless "transformer". Every payment uses a one-time code, so a recorded signal can't be replayed.

Sources: Wikipedia "Near-field communication" and "Contactless payment"; Apple Pay security overview; EMVCo.

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 26 · Your toilet doesn't push the water down. It sucks it. 🚽 In most North American toilets, the bowl fills the curved trapway so fast that the whole pipe turns into a siphon, and that gurgle at the end is air breaking it. Puller or pusher: which one is yours?

Sources: Wikipedia "Flush toilet" and "Low-flush toilet"; US EPA WaterSense (Energy Policy Act 1992, 1.6 gpf); Explain That Stuff "How toilets work"; plumbing guides on bucket flushing (Benjamin Franklin Plumbing, HomeServe); Architizer "How to Specify: Toilets".

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 27 · That tiny hole at the bottom of a plane window isn't a flaw. Windows have three panes. The hole in the middle one lets cabin air into the gap, so the pressure pushing out lands on the outer pane, with the middle pane as a backup. It also lets moisture out so the window doesn't fog up.

Sources: ScienceAlert; Time (quoting Slate's Mark Vanhoenacker and GKN Aerospace's Marlowe Moncur); AirHelp.

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 28 · A hurricane is a giant heat engine, and its fuel is warm ocean water. The sea surface needs to be at least about 27 °C (80 °F). Warm, moist air rises, cools and condenses into storm clouds, releasing the heat that powers the storm. Earth's rotation turns the inflow into a spin: counterclockwise north of the equator, clockwise south of it. When sustained winds reach 74 mph it is officially a hurricane, with a calm eye inside an eyewall of the strongest winds. Which part surprised you most?

Sources: NOAA "Hurricanes"; NOAA JetStream "Tropical Cyclone Introduction" and "Tropical Cyclone Structure"; NHC Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale.

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 29 · To dive, a submarine lets the ocean in, on purpose. 🌊 So how does it ever come back up? Vents open, air rushes out, seawater floods the ballast tanks and it slips under. Trim tanks make it hover, diving planes steer, and a blast of compressed air pushes the water back out to bring it home. Would you trust a bubble of air to bring you home?

Sources: Wikipedia "Submarine", "Ballast tank", "Archimedes' principle", "Swim bladder", "Virginia-class submarine".

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 30 · Your WiFi goes through walls. How? It isn't pushing anything solid. It's radio waves, about 12 cm from peak to peak, and a wall is barely in their way. Each wall just takes a small share, and metal, stone and water take the most. The 5 GHz band is faster but reaches less far.

Sources: Wikipedia "Wi-Fi" and "Microwave oven"; basic physics (c = f x wavelength).

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 31 · Why do onions make you cry? The onion isn't sad, it's defending itself. Cutting rips its cells open, so enzymes meet sulfur chemicals and make a stinging gas, syn-propanethial-S-oxide. The gas drifts into your eyes, your nerves warn your brain, and your tear glands flush it away.

Sources: Wikipedia "Lachrymatory factor"; Discover Magazine; The Conversation; Imai et al., Nature 2002.

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 32 · When you sleep, your brain doesn't switch off. It runs through cycles of about 80 to 100 minutes, four to six times a night: deep slow-wave sleep early on, more REM later, when your eyes dart, your brain is about as active as when you're awake, and dreaming usually happens. Sleep helps form long-term memories, and in mice, researchers found the brain clears waste faster while asleep.

Sources: NHLBI/NIH (Stages of Sleep; Why Is Sleep Important?); Xie et al., Science 2013 (mouse study); Discover Magazine (why we dream is still debated).

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 33 · Why is snow white if ice is clear? There's no white in snow at all. A snowbank is mostly air, packed with tiny clear ice crystals. Light bounces off and bends through crystal after crystal, and since ice barely absorbs visible light, every colour comes back out together: white. A smashed windowpane does the same thing. But poke a deep hole in fresh snow and it glows blue, because deep snow soaks up a little more red light. ❄️

Sources: NSIDC (National Snow and Ice Data Center), "Science of snow"; UCAR Center for Science Education; Live Science (Kenneth Libbrecht, Caltech).

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 34 · Why are yawns contagious? Scientists still argue. Just thinking about yawning can set one off. Dogs can catch human yawns (21 of 29 in one study, though later results were mixed), and some chimps yawn at videos of yawning chimps. Idea 1: brain cooling. With a cold pack on the forehead, people caught far fewer yawns (9% vs 41%). Idea 2: it's social, since yawns spread most among family. But the empathy link is contested: in 328 people, catching yawns tracked age, not empathy. 🥱

Sources: Gallup & Gallup, Evolutionary Psychology (2007); Gallup & Eldakar, Frontiers in Neuroscience (2013); Norscia & Palagi, PLoS ONE (2011); Bartholomew & Cirulli, PLoS ONE (2014); Joly-Mascheroni et al., Biology Letters (2008); Anderson et al. (2004); Provine, American Scientist (2005).

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 35 · Why do your fingers wrinkle in water? It's not just soggy skin: your nerves do it. Doctors noticed in the 1930s that fingers with a damaged median nerve stay smooth in water. In a warm soak, nerves make the tiny blood vessels under your fingertips narrow, the volume drops, and the skin on top is pulled into folds, only on hairless skin like fingertips, palms and soles. A 2025 study even found the same fingers wrinkle in the same pattern every time. Why? The leading idea is grip, but the studies disagree. Did you think it was just soggy skin?

Sources: Haseleu et al., PLoS ONE (2014); Wilder-Smith & Chow, Muscle & Nerve (2003); Kareklas, Nettle & Smulders, Biology Letters (2013); Binghamton University (2025).

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 36 · How do hand warmers get hot with no battery? The recipe is on the maker's own safety sheet: more than half iron powder, plus water, a pinch of salt, activated charcoal and vermiculite. Tear the pack open, air gets in through the cloth, and the iron starts to rust. Rusting always gives off heat; fine powder and salt just make it fast enough to feel, for hours. The clicky reusable kind is different: a liquid holding more dissolved salt than it normally could, which crystallises and releases stored heat when you click it. 🔥🧤

Sources: Kobayashi Healthcare safety data sheet (air-activated heating packs); University of Silesia (Prof. Robert Musioł); Minnesota State University, Mankato (Dr. Marie Pomije, via KTTC); BBC Science Focus.

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 37 · How does a thermos keep drinks hot and cold? It has no idea which one it's holding. It doesn't make heat or cold; it just stops heat crossing, both ways. Heat travels by conduction, convection and radiation. The gap between a thermos's two walls is a near-vacuum, so heat can't conduct across and no air currents can carry it, and the silvered walls bounce infrared back. The weak point is the top, where the walls join, which is why the neck is narrow and the stopper is thick. James Dewar showed the idea in London on Christmas Day 1892, to keep liquid gases cold, and never patented it. Coffee or ice water in yours?

Sources: University of Sydney School of Physics (Thermos Flask); Royal Institution (Dewar flask, 1892); Encyclopaedia Britannica (vacuum bottle).

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 38 · Why does popcorn pop? Each kernel holds a little water (about 13-14.5%) inside a tough hull. Heat it and the water gets hotter than boiling, the starch turns to gel, and at about 180 °C the pressure reaches around ten times normal air pressure. The hull cracks, the steam bursts out and the gel puffs into foam that sets solid in hundredths of a second. The pop sound? High-speed video shows it lines up with the steam rushing out, not the crack. 🍿

Sources: Virot & Ponomarenko, J. R. Soc. Interface (2015); Hoseney et al., Journal of Cereal Science (1983); Purdue University Agriculture (Hamaker, 2020).

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 39 · Why can you see your breath when it's cold? Your breath is always full of water, as invisible water vapor. Warm air can hold lots of it, but air at freezing holds only about a tenth as much as air as warm as your body. So when your warm, wet breath hits the cold, it cools past its dew point, and the vapor sticks together into tiny droplets of liquid water: a little cloud. Real clouds form the same way, just way bigger. A second later it mixes with more dry air, and the droplets evaporate again. ☁️❄️

Sources: University of Washington, Dept. of Atmospheric Sciences; NOAA National Weather Service (dew point, JetStream "How clouds form"); Library of Congress, Everyday Mysteries.

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 40 · Why do you get more static shocks in winter? Every time your socks or shoes rub the carpet, tiny electrons hop from one material to the other, and your body piles up charge, up to thousands of volts (but only a tiny amount of charge, so it's just a sting). On humid days, a thin film of water on surfaces quietly drains that charge away. Cold winter air holds very little water, and heating it indoors doesn't add any, so the charge has nowhere to go... until you touch the doorknob. ⚡🚪

Sources: University of Kentucky Dept. of Physics & Astronomy; University of Wisconsin-Madison Physics ("Wonders of Physics"); University of Alaska Fairbanks Geophysical Institute (Alaska Science Forum); Northeastern University.

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 41 · Why does your stomach growl? It can growl even when you're not hungry. It's your gut squeezing: muscle waves called peristalsis push food, fluid and gas through your stomach and small intestine, and the gas and fluid gurgle as they're squeezed through. The ancient Greeks called it borborygmi, "rumbling". It's often loudest when you're empty, because there's no food to muffle it. Once your stomach is empty, a cleaning wave sweeps through, roughly every couple of hours while you fast, driven by a hormone called motilin, which some researchers link to hunger. Its cousin ghrelin rises right before meals. Does yours growl at the worst moment?

Sources: Takahashi 2012 (J Neurogastroenterol Motil, migrating motor complex); Tack et al. 2016 (Gut, motilin and hunger); Cummings et al. 2001 (Diabetes, ghrelin before meals); Scientific American.

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 42 · How do cats purr? Scientists still argue about it. One side says the brain sets a rhythm and muscles in the larynx, the voice box, twitch about 20 to 30 times a second, so the vocal folds open and snap shut and chop the air into a rumble, breathing in and breathing out. But in 2023, researchers in Vienna blew air through cat voice boxes in a lab with no nerves or muscles working, and they still purred at 25 to 30 times a second. Soft pads of tissue inside the vocal folds make them heavy, so they vibrate slowly, which is how a small cat makes such a deep sound. Muscles or pads? Probably both. And cats don't only purr when happy: they purr at the vet, when hurt, mother cats purr while nursing, and some hide a cry inside the purr to ask for food. Is your cat a loud purrer?

Sources: Herbst et al. 2023 (Current Biology, purring without neural input); Remmers & Gautier 1972 (Respiration Physiology); McComb et al. 2009 (Current Biology, the cry embedded within the purr); University of Vienna.

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 43 · Why do you get brain freeze? 🍦 Your brain isn't freezing. Brain tissue has no pain sensors. The cold hits the roof of your mouth, and the leading idea is that the blood vessels there tighten, then swing wide open. A small 2012 study suggests an artery at the front of the brain widens fast as the pain hits. The trigeminal nerve carries the signal, and your brain blames your forehead: referred pain. Fix: press your tongue to the roof of your mouth.

Sources: Serrador et al., Experimental Biology 2012 (abstract); Kaczorowski & Kaczorowski, BMJ (2002); Cleveland Clinic; Houston Methodist.

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 44 · Why do your ears pop on a plane? That pop is a tiny bubble of air squeezing through your Eustachian tube, the pencil-lead-thin door to the air pocket behind your eardrum. Up high, the cabin is kept like a mountain town, so on the climb the air in your ear pushes out. On the way down the cabin pressure climbs back up, air has to get *in*, and the tube only opens when you swallow, yawn or chew. That's why landing is the hard part, and why babies cry near the end of a flight. ✈️ (Educational only, not medical advice.)

Sources: Stony Brook Medicine Otolaryngology, "Ears and Altitude"; CDC Yellow Book, "Air travel"; MedlinePlus, "Ear barotrauma"; KidsHealth (Nemours), "Flying and your child's ears"; Mirza & Richardson, J Laryngol Otol 2005; FAA 14 CFR 25.841.

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 45 · Why does your nose run when it's cold? Your nose is the air conditioner for your lungs: it warms and wets every breath. Cold winter air is usually very dry, so nerves in your nose raise the alarm, your brain sends extra blood to warm the air, and tiny glands pump out more mucus and water, often more than it needs, so the extra drips out. A second drip comes from your warm, wet breath hitting the cold tip of your nose and condensing, like breath fogging a cold window. Doctors call it cold-induced rhinitis, or "skier's nose". 🤧❄️

Sources: Dr. Mitchell Grayson, Medical College of Wisconsin (via Smithsonian); David King, University of Queensland (The Conversation); Dr. Andrew Lane, Johns Hopkins Sinus Center (NPR).

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 46 · Why is ice slippery? Not because your weight melts it. The old "pressure melting" answer from 1886 only gets ice down to about -3.5 °C, yet people skate at -35 °C, and you can slip standing still. Friction heat melts a thin film while you move, and the surface of ice isn't quite solid: in 2018 researchers found loose top molecules rolling across it like tiny spheres, with ice slipperiest around -7 °C. A 2025 simulation suggests rubbing scrambles the surface without melting it. The exact mix is still debated. ⛸️

Sources: R. Rosenberg, "Why Is Ice Slippery?", Physics Today (2005); Weber et al., J. Phys. Chem. Lett. (2018) and University of Amsterdam news; Atila, Sukhomlinov & Müser, Phys. Rev. Lett. (2025).

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 47 · Why do snowflakes have six sides? It starts with one water molecule: one oxygen and two hydrogens in a bent little V. When water freezes, hydrogen bonds lock the molecules into rings of six, ring after ring, a honeycomb of ice. So every snow crystal starts as a tiny six-sided prism, and as it grows, branches sprout from its six corners. The six arms match because they grow at the same time through the same air, and no two flakes fall the same path, so no two look exactly alike. ❄️

Sources: Kenneth Libbrecht, Caltech (SnowCrystals.com, "Snowflake Science"); Caltech News, "Snowflake Science"; KQED Deep Look (with Libbrecht); NSIDC.

Follow for more of how it really works.

Ep. 48 · Why do eggs turn solid when you cook them? 🍳 Egg white is almost 90% water with folded-up proteins floating in it. Heat makes the proteins unfold (denature), then the loose chains grab each other and tangle into a mesh that traps the water, so clear and runny turn white and solid. The white starts to set around 63 °C and the yolk around 70 °C. Can you uncook one? In 2015, chemists refolded one egg-white protein with a vortex machine. Not the whole egg, but it's a step toward cheaper proteins for medicine.

Sources: Exploratorium (Science of Cooking); Harold McGee, On Food and Cooking; UC Irvine News (2015); USDA FoodData Central.

Ep. 49 · Why do leaves change color in the fall? All summer, leaves are full of green chlorophyll, which turns sunlight into food. As nights get longer, trees stop making it and the green breaks down, revealing yellow and orange carotenoids that were there all along. Reds are different: most anthocyanins are made fresh in the fall, when a cork-like layer at the leaf stem traps sugar and bright sun helps turn it red. That's why warm sunny days and cool nights give the brightest reds. Brown tannins come last, then the leaf lets go. Red or gold?

Sources: USDA Forest Service; Purdue, Utah State and Clemson extension.

Ep. 50 · How does a candle actually burn? The wick isn't the fuel: the wax is, as a gas. The flame's heat melts a cup of wax at the top, the liquid climbs the wick like water up a towel, and near the flame it turns into vapour. That vapour is what burns. Michael Faraday showed it in his 1860 lectures for young people: blow a candle out, light the smoke, and a trail of fire runs down and relights the wick. The dark core of the flame is vapour that hasn't burned yet; the yellow glow is tiny specks of solid carbon, so hot they shine. It all ends up as water and carbon dioxide. Have you ever relit a candle through its smoke?

Source: Michael Faraday, The Chemical History of a Candle (Royal Institution lectures, 1860-61).

Ep. 51 · Why does the time change mess with your sleep? Your wall clock jumps an hour in a second, but your body's master clock (the SCN, a cluster of nerve cells in your brain) is set by light and shifts slowly. Left alone it runs a bit long, about 24 hours and 10 minutes, so shifting later (fall back) is easy and shifting earlier (spring forward) is hard. One study found sleep adjusted after fall back but not after spring forward, especially for night owls, and US fatal car crashes rose about 6% the week after spring forward, with no rise after fall back. 🕰️ (Educational only, not medical advice.)

Sources: NIH NIGMS "Circadian Rhythms"; Czeisler et al., Science (1999); Kantermann et al., Current Biology (2007); Fritz et al., Current Biology (2020); American Academy of Sleep Medicine position statement (2020).

Ep. 52 · Can you really smell snow coming? Sort of. Snow is frozen water, and pure water has no smell. Cold air slows odor molecules, so there are simply fewer smells around (Monell scientist Pamela Dalton). Humid air before a storm may help your nose, though lab studies disagree. The strongest clue is a feeling, not a smell: nerve endings in your nose carry a cold sensor (TRPM8, the one menthol switches on), and Monell researchers found the fresh feeling of breathing comes mostly from your nose lining cooling down. ❄️

Sources: Monell Chemical Senses Center (Dalton, via Discovery News; Zhao et al., PLoS One 2011); Kuehn et al. (2008) and Drews et al. (2021), Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol; Ordás et al., J Comp Neurol (2021).

Ep. 53 · Why does a microwave have a metal mesh on the door? 🍿 The oven's waves are about 12 cm long, and the mesh holes are only a few millimetres across, much too small for them to squeeze through, so the metal bounces them back inside (the idea behind a Faraday cage). Visible light's waves are less than a thousandth of a millimetre, so they slip right through and you can watch your food. Bonus: the trapped waves make hot and cold spots about 6 cm apart, which is why the plate spins.

Sources: Swinburne University of Technology; University of Arizona Optical Sciences outreach; The Open University (OpenLearn).

Ep. 54 · Do goldfish really have a 3-second memory? 🐟 Not even close. At the University of Plymouth, goldfish learned to work a lever that fed them only one hour a day, and they crowded it just before feeding time. In Israel, fish trained to a feeding sound reportedly still came back to it months after release. In Japan, goldfish even learned to tell Bach from Stravinsky. Fish researcher Culum Brown says goldfish memories can last weeks, months, even years.

Sources: Gee, Stephenson & Wright, J. Exp. Anal. Behav. (1994); Shinozuka, Ono & Watanabe, Behavioural Processes (2013); Live Science (Culum Brown, Macquarie University).

Ep. 55 · Why do we get goosebumps? Under every hair is a tiny muscle, the arrector pili. When you get cold, a nerve tells it to squeeze: the hair stands up and the skin bunches into a bump. On a furry animal that fluffs the coat and traps warm air; on us, with most of the fur gone, it's mostly a leftover. The twist: Harvard scientists found the same nerve also connects to the stem cells that grow hair, and in mice a long cold spell made it fire harder and grow fur faster. 🐈❄️

Sources: Shwartz et al. (Hsu lab, Harvard), Cell 2020; New York Stem Cell Foundation; ScienceAlert on the Harvard release; Science News Explores.

Ep. 56 · Does hot water really freeze faster than cold? The idea goes back to Aristotle, Bacon and Descartes, and it's named after Erasto Mpemba, a Tanzanian schoolboy whose hot ice-cream mix froze first. In 1969 he and physicist Denis Osborne published tests where hot water started freezing first. But careful tests in 2016 found no real evidence for it, and showed that moving a thermometer just 1 cm can flip the result. Evaporation, dissolved gas, currents and supercooling might matter in some freezers. Honest answer: sometimes, maybe, and scientists still argue. 🧊🔥

Sources: Burridge & Linden, "Questioning the Mpemba effect", Scientific Reports (2016); Mpemba & Osborne, "Cool?", Physics Education (1969).

Ep. 57 · How do noise-cancelling headphones work? They fight sound with more sound. Tiny microphones hear the noise, a chip flips that wave upside down, and the speaker plays this "anti-noise" with your music. When a squeeze meets a stretch, they cancel. It works best on slow, steady hums like a plane engine or an air conditioner (long waves, so a tiny delay barely matters). Voices and sudden sounds change too fast, so the earcup padding does that job. The idea was first patented in 1936.

Sources: Elliott & Nelson, Active Noise Control review (ISVR, University of Southampton); Sennheiser ANC notes.

Ep. 58 · Why can't you taste food when you have a cold? Your tongue works fine: it only senses a few basic tastes, like sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami. Everything else, strawberry, coffee, garlic, is smell, drifting up a channel at the back of your mouth into your nose (retronasal smell). With a cold, swelling and mucus stop those smells reaching the smell cells high in your nose, so food tastes bland. Try the jellybean test: pinch your nose and chew, it's just sweet. Let go, and suddenly it's cherry. Have you tried the nose-pinch test?

Sources: NIH / NIDCD taste and smell disorder fact sheets; Monell Chemical Senses Center.

Ep. 59 · Why do we get hiccups? 😮 Your diaphragm (the muscle under your lungs) suddenly jerks, and about a thirtieth of a second later your vocal cords snap shut: "hic!". It's a reflex loop through the vagus and phrenic nerves. What hiccups are for is still a mystery: one idea says they help babies burp out swallowed air; scientists also suspect they're a leftover from gill-breathing ancestors, like tadpoles. The cures? There's no proof they work for everyone. Hiccups lasting more than 2 days? See a doctor.

Sources: Howes, BioEssays (2012); Straus et al., BioEssays (2003); NHS.

Ep. 60 · Why does aluminum foil have a shiny side and a dull side? ✨ Blame the factory. Foil is rolled thinner and thinner between polished steel rollers, and on the last pass two sheets go through together so the thin foil doesn't tear. The outsides touch the polished rollers and come out shiny; the insides only touch each other and come out matte. Does the side matter for cooking? Reynolds and Germany's aluminium industry association both say no. The exception is non-stick foil: its coating is on the dull side.

Sources: GDA (German aluminium industry association) foil factsheet; Reynolds Kitchens.

Ep. 61 · Why do planes leave white trails in the sky? ✈️ It isn't smoke: the plane is making a cloud. Burning jet fuel makes carbon dioxide and lots of water vapor. At cruising height the air can be as cold as -70 °F, so the vapor condenses on tiny specks and freezes into ice crystals, like your breath on a cold day. Whether a trail lasts depends on the sky, not the plane: in dry air the ice evaporates within seconds to minutes, while in humid air the crystals keep growing and the trail can last for hours or spread into thin cirrus cloud. And no, they're not "chemtrails": in a 2016 survey, 76 of 77 atmospheric scientists had seen no evidence of secret spraying.

Sources: EPA/FAA/NOAA Contrails Fact Sheet; NASA contrails educator guide; Shearer et al., Environmental Research Letters (2016), UC Irvine & Carnegie Institution.

Ep. 62 · Why do wet dogs smell so bad? 🐕💧 It's not really the dog, it's who lives on it. A dog's skin and fur are home to normal, healthy bacteria and yeast, and a Texas A&M vet study found furry skin carries the richest mix of microbes. Those microbes give off tiny smelly molecules. On a dry dog they mostly stay put, but water knocks them loose from the fur, and as it evaporates it carries them up to your nose. In one small pilot study, wet dog hair had 22 key odor compounds vs 16 when dry: some mushroomy, some fruity or floral... and some fecal.

Sources: American Chemical Society, Reactions (2015); Rodrigues Hoffmann et al., PLoS ONE (2014), Texas A&M College of Veterinary Medicine; Young et al., WSAVA Congress (2002).

Ep. 64 · Why do cats knead? It starts in the first days of life: a nursing kitten presses its mother's belly, which helps release oxytocin and get the milk flowing. Push, milk, warmth and safety all arrive together, and grown-up cats keep the habit (scientists call that neoteny). The leading theory: kneading still feels like that comfort, which is why it so often comes with purring. Theory two: cats have scent glands in their paw pads, so each press may leave an invisible "this one's mine". Theory three: wild cats trampled grass into a soft bed. If the kneading turns frantic or nonstop, ask your vet. 🐈🍪

Sources: Hazel & Henning (School of Animal and Veterinary Science, University of Adelaide), "Why do cats knead?", The Conversation; VCA Animal Hospitals; Vetstreet.

Ep. 65 · Why does your voice sound weird on recordings? When you talk, your voice reaches your ears two ways: through the air, and through your skull (bone conduction), which boosts the low, deep tones. So in your head you sound deeper and fuller. A microphone only hears the air path, so the recording sounds thinner and higher, and that's the voice everyone else hears. In a 2023 study, people picked out their own voice more easily when it played through bone-conduction headphones. Do you like your voice on recordings?

Sources: Tim Hullar, Washington University School of Medicine (Scientific American); Orepic et al., Royal Society Open Science (2023).

Ep. 66 · How does a refrigerator keep food cold? It doesn't make cold, it moves heat. A refrigerant runs round a loop: inside, it's cold and at low pressure, so it boils and soaks up heat from your food. The compressor squeezes it until it's hotter than your kitchen, and the coils on the back dump that heat into the room. Then it squeezes through a tiny valve, expands, and gets cold again. That's why the back of your fridge feels warm. Air conditioners and heat pumps use the same trick.

Sources: Penn State EGEE 102 "Refrigerators"; US EPA "Heat Pumps".

Ep. 67 · Why does cracking your knuckles make a pop? Nothing breaks. Your knuckle is a capsule of joint fluid, and when you pull the bones apart the pressure drops, gas comes out of the fluid and a cavity snaps open. In 2015 researchers filmed it inside an MRI: the cavity formed at the moment of the crack and stayed afterwards. A 2018 model says a partial collapse could make the same sound, so the debate isn't settled. It takes about half an hour to crack the same knuckle again. And arthritis? One doctor cracked only his left hand for 60+ years and won an Ig Nobel Prize for finding no difference. 🖐️ (Educational only, not medical advice.)

Sources: Kawchuk et al., PLOS ONE (2015); Chandran Suja & Barakat, Scientific Reports (2018); Unger, Arthritis & Rheumatism (1998) / Ig Nobel 2009; Castellanos & Axelrod, Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases (1990); Arthritis UK.

Ep. 68 · How do planes actually stay in the air? Not because air on top has "farther to go": NASA calls the equal-transit idea one of the most widely circulated, incorrect explanations, and smoke tests show the top air reaches the back first. A curved, tilted wing turns a huge amount of air downward, and by Newton's third law the air pushes the wing up. Turning the flow also leaves lower pressure above the wing and higher below. Both descriptions are true at the same time. ✈️

Sources: NASA Glenn Research Center, Beginner's Guide to Aeronautics ("Equal Transit Theory", "What is Lift?"); University of Cambridge, Holger Babinsky (Physics Education 2003; "How wings really work", 2012); Scientific American (2020).

Ep. 69 · How does your phone's GPS know where you are? About thirty GPS satellites circle the Earth twice a day, 20,200 km up, each broadcasting where it is and what time it is. Your phone times how long each signal takes to arrive, turns that into a distance, and with at least four satellites pins your spot (trilateration). The twist: the timing has to be perfect, so each satellite carries an atomic clock, and relativity makes those clocks gain about 38 microseconds a day. Without correcting for it, your position would drift by about 10 km a day.

Sources: GPS.gov (Space Segment); Richard Pogge, Ohio State University, "GPS and Relativity".

Ep. 71 · Why do we sneeze? It's a reflex. When dust, pollen or a germ irritates the lining of your nose, the trigeminal nerve signals your brainstem (scientists think a "sneeze centre" sits there), and the same routine runs every time: eyes shut, a deep breath, pressure, then a blast that washes the irritants out. About one in four people also sneeze in bright light (the photic sneeze reflex), and nobody knows exactly why. And no, your heart doesn't stop: the chest pressure can briefly change its rhythm, but the electrical signal keeps going. 🤧☀️

Sources: Seijo-Martínez et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry (2006); Wang et al., Scientific Reports (2019); UAMS Health (University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences).

Ep. 75 · What is earwax actually for? 👂 It isn't dirt, it's your ear's built-in cleaner. Glands in the ear canal make a waxy oil called cerumen. It traps dust and germs, keeps the skin moist and even fights bacteria. Old wax rides out on a conveyor belt: the skin of the canal slowly moves outward from the eardrum, chewing and talking help it along, and at the opening it dries, flakes and falls out. That's why ear doctors say to skip the cotton swabs, which mostly push wax deeper. Sticky vs flaky wax comes down to one letter in one gene, ABCC11, and dry wax is most common in East Asia.

Sources: AAO-HNS Clinical Practice Guideline: Earwax (2017); AAO-HNS ENT Health; MedlinePlus; Yoshiura et al., Nature Genetics (2006).

Ep. 76 · Why do we blink so much? About 15 times a minute (American Academy of Ophthalmology), more often than your eyes strictly need for wetting. Each blink spreads tears across the eye, and on a screen your rate can drop to about 5-7 a minute. So scientists asked when we blink: people watching the same video blinked together, at calm moments like the end of an action or when the main character left the screen. A brain-scan study then found that right after a blink, attention areas dipped while the default mode network (a resting network) became more active, and simply blacking out the screen didn't do the same. One idea: blinks may work as tiny breaks for your attention. These are findings, not settled facts. 👁️

Sources: American Academy of Ophthalmology; Nakano et al., Proceedings of the Royal Society B (2009); Nakano et al., PNAS (2013, online Dec 2012); Osaka University press release.
